body.text: Can Labor cash in on AI and data centres without paying the US political price?
As anyone with a relative who has slipped into the anti-data centre algorithm can attest, there are some truly bonkers myths out there.

Spend five minutes scrolling and you too could become convinced electromagnetic fields are killing all the bees, while the low-frequency noise emanating from the giant computing stacks is giving tinnitus to entire towns.
But not all the effects of data centres are imagined, as many residents across the US have learned.
From huge volumes of unaccounted water consumption to soaring electricity bills, there are ample cases to illustrate some fears are very real.
It's why data centres became a politically potent cost-of-living and local community issue in the US midterms, helping reshape gubernatorial campaigns in Texas, Georgia and Ohio.

The strongest evidence of direct voter rejection occurred at an even more local level, where dozens of ballot measures restricting data centres were approved in communities across California, Illinois, Maine, New York and other states.

While US politicians ignored the risks of the AI boom at their own peril, the same cannot be said for Australia, where most MPs have a well-worn script about capitalising on the upside while mitigating the bad.
But that political consensus could prove fragile once the enormous sums of money being promised are weighed against the much more immediate concerns of voters.
Getting ahead of the backlash
After a few false starts, the federal government has at least recognised the danger early enough to try to avoid the worst of the US experience.

There is broad agreement in Canberra that tech companies seeking to build in Australia must bring their own energy supply, efficiently and transparently manage water usage and consult with the community.
The challenge is in how to realise those broad principles in practice.
In just a few weeks, a parliamentary committee examining all these issues will hand down its final report.
That work, along with a rapid review into the OpenAI Medicare data breach, will feed into national AI standards flagged by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in July.

As Labor's self-imposed, end-of-year deadline to unveil the detailed proposal looms, the US results offer a timely reminder that the economic promise of artificial intelligence will count for little if voters see no benefit.

In some respects, the data centre backlash in the US has only strengthened Australia's bargaining position with tech giants scrambling to find safe harbour for their billions of dollars in investment.
That does not mean voters here are yet convinced that whatever Australia actually gets out of hosting the infrastructure will be worth the cost.
Limits of political consensus
This explains why the Commonwealth and states are placing a premium on community consultation, particularly with regards to where data centres are located.
Though no-one is suggesting these giant structures will be taking up prime housing or agricultural land, suggestions there will be none in the "suburbs" likely depends on definition.
Those vehemently opposed to data centres would say any proposal within cooee of a residential street was unacceptable.
But to rule out construction in the many industrial areas interspersed through Australia's towns and cities, including near houses, would be impractical.
It's the sort of semantics that mean, even with settled national standards, the risk of local backlash will remain high going forward.
As for concerns about electricity and water, the broad political agreement on protecting consumers conceals some fairly fundamental disagreements about how to do it.

National cabinet has papered over divisions on energy, with Queensland Premier David Crisafulli confident coal-powered data centres can meet requirements to protect electricity consumers, while federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen insists only renewables will stack up.
Those following AI closely argue that water consumption can be significantly mitigated through advances in cooling technologies, but the sheer scale of the projects is staggering.
Sydney Water has warned the industry could consume up to a quarter of the city's drinking water by 2035.

Queensland initially stood alone in rejecting minimum water standards proposed by federal Water Minister Murray Watt, including requirements to minimise consumption, report usage and pay for infrastructure.
But the Crisafulli government subsequently signed up to the national standards, perhaps realising how exposed the state would be if things went wrong.
All politics is local
All signs suggest the national AI standards have a bipartisan path through the parliament, but signing up is much easier in the abstract.
Where there are real-life proposals, consensus can quickly fray.
Take the agreement signed by AI company Anthropic to use part of a $32 billion data centre proposed near Dalby, about 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

Liberal federal member for Groom, Garth Hamilton, last month broke ranks with his party to voice his concerns that locals were not being heard, revealing the proposed data centre was frequently raised "unprompted" by voters in his community.

In July, Labor minister Sam Rae and neighbouring federal MP Alice Jordan-Baird released a statement critical of a plan by Syncline Energy to develop a 350-hectare, 2.4GW data centre in Plumpton in Melbourne's outer north-west.

The pair noted community concerns about the potential impact on energy, water, traffic and ongoing noise, stating they would not support developments that failed to meet the government's expectations around those issues.
The problem there is the project is progressing ahead of standards that do not yet exist and are due to be legislated only next year.
This scenario is precisely why some members of the crossbench and the Greens are supportive of a moratorium on new projects until the prospective AI laws are in place.
For now, Labor is resisting that approach, effectively asking communities to trust that the promised safeguards will arrive in time.
The price of playing AI host
Even if Australia gets everything right on data centre construction, there is still the question of how the country can extract ongoing value as a computer host.
Independent ACT senator David Pocock wants an immediate 5 per cent levy on all data centres to guarantee Australia a slice of the economic value.

Labor has long argued Australia needs to participate in the higher-value parts of the AI industry, with Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton raising the prospect of securing computing power to support homegrown innovation.

He has drawn comparisons with Australia's gas boom, where governments made the mistake of allowing an enormous export industry to develop without locking in sufficient benefits for domestic consumers.
It's a reminder and a warning that attracting investment is not the same as securing a return on it.
As it stands, Australia is still well placed to benefit from the rush to cash in on the AI boom that has sparked fierce backlash in the US.
But it is not immune from the political forces that turned a technological gold rush into an electoral liability.
